segment_name: Opening: The Weight of the Vernon Fortune

questions.question: Eleanor, you described Oliphant's structure as almost geometrical — Catherine's bitterness in one chapter, Hester's entrapment in the next, like mirror images of each other. Can you read us the passage from c8:p5 and walk us through what you mean? Because I want listeners to actually hear what you're hearing in the syntax.
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read the c8:p5 passage aloud and articulate the structural doubling argument — this opens the segment with a close reading rather than an abstract claim, and sets up the Catherine/Hester comparison that all three experts care about

questions.question: Caroline, you heard Eleanor there — but you said in our chat beforehand that c8:p5 is less about Hester's potential than about sheer grinding impossibility. Is that a difference of emphasis, or do you two actually disagree about what Oliphant is doing with Hester in this opening?
questions.intent: Surface the Caroline/Eleanor tension about whether Hester's constraint is tragic or whether Hester's own rigidity is part of the problem — push Caroline to sharpen her 'constraint over escape' reading against Eleanor's more structural take

questions.question: James, I want to bring you in on Catherine, because you used a phrase that stuck with me — you called her 'the most rational actor in the room.' Can you read us that line from c7:p9, the 'what did it matter' line, and make the case? Because on first hearing it sounds pretty cold.
questions.intent: Get James to read and defend the c7:p9 passage, making the rational-actor argument for Catherine's cynicism — this is the most counterintuitive take in the room and will provoke both Caroline and Eleanor

questions.question: Caroline, you wanted to read the passage about everyone taking from Catherine — the biblical one, 'eaten of her bread, drunk of her cup' — and you described it as almost liturgical. But James just told us it's the language of parasitism. Are those the same reading or completely different ones?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Caroline's 'liturgical sacrifice' reading and James's 'parasitism' reading of the same passage from c40:p30 — both experts flagged this quote but for very different emotional registers

questions.question: Eleanor, here's the thing I keep coming back to — all three of you are saying Catherine and Hester are trapped by the same system, just at different ends of it. But if that's true, why does the novel set them up as antagonists? Is Oliphant asking us to see through that conflict, or is the conflict itself the point?
questions.intent: Push Eleanor to synthesize the generational-echo argument into a claim about the novel's larger design — this question is designed to produce either a strong agreement that escalates into something more interesting, or a three-way disagreement about whether Oliphant is offering critique or just documentation

steering_notes: This segment should feel like it's building toward one big unresolved question: does Oliphant want us to sympathize, analyze, or indict? Keep returning to the actual language — push for readings aloud wherever possible. The Caroline/Eleanor tension about Hester (tragic constraint vs. her own rigidity) is the most productive disagreement and might need a second push if it doesn't ignite naturally after question two. James's rational-actor framing is the most provocative and should be let loose early enough that the other two have time to respond. Don't let the conversation stay abstract — every time someone says 'structure' or 'system,' ask them to point to a sentence.
cross_engagement_targets: Caroline reads Catherine's cynicism as adaptive survival mechanism; Eleanor reads it as trauma calcifying into architecture — these sound similar but Caroline emphasizes psychological necessity while Eleanor emphasizes structural function. Worth surfacing explicitly.

James and Eleanor appear to agree that Catherine's indifference is not moral failure, but James predicted Eleanor would call it decline — check whether that disagreement still exists or whether they've converged, and if so push James on where his reading actually differs from Eleanor's.

Eleanor wants to push back on Hester's self-perceived entrapment, suggesting her 'high-spirited nature is itself a rigidity' — this directly contradicts Caroline's deep sympathy for Hester's constraint. This is the sharpest latent disagreement in the room and should be drawn out explicitly in question two or revisited at the close.

segment_name: The Architecture of Ambition: Hester's Constrained Desires

questions.question: Eleanor, you've talked about Oliphant repeating this physical language—'breast swelled,' 'breath came short,' 'fires in her eyes'—almost like a pressure building up with nowhere to go. Can you read us the c30:p31 passage and say what you think Oliphant is actually doing technically there? Because it feels like more than just emotional description.
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read c30:p31 aloud and make the case for free indirect discourse as a structural trap, not just atmosphere—sets up the central question of whether this is craft or critique

questions.question: Caroline, you've got this line you want us to hear—'it was not a little money that Hester wanted, but work of which something good might come.' You said that's the key to everything. Why? Because James might say the whole point is that without money the work question is moot anyway—so are you two actually disagreeing about what Hester's tragedy *is*?
questions.intent: Force Caroline to defend the moral-agency reading against James's structural-exclusion reading—surface the real disagreement between them about whether Hester's problem is philosophical or economic

questions.question: James, you called c36:p91 a legal question—'if you're held responsible for outcomes you don't control, do you have any rights at all?' That's a striking way to put it. But Caroline's going to say that framing almost makes Hester sound like a plaintiff, when what Oliphant is doing is something more tender than that. Are you deliberately stripping the sentiment out, and if so, why?
questions.intent: Provoke James to defend his hard-nosed structural reading against Caroline's tenderness argument—and potentially get him to concede that Oliphant holds both registers simultaneously

questions.question: Eleanor, you want to push back on James reading c8:p13—'a heart made to believe and trust, yet warped to almost all around'—as a moral failing. But here's the thing: James isn't actually saying it's a moral failing, he's saying the *system* warps her. Isn't that exactly what you're saying too? Or is there a real difference between your readings there?
questions.intent: Test whether Eleanor and James's apparent agreement conceals a genuine disagreement—Eleanor focuses on interiority and narrative form, James on institutional structure; force them to locate the actual difference

questions.question: Caroline, you said we shouldn't forgive the novel for not answering Hester's question. That's a strong thing to say about a book you clearly love. Eleanor thinks the novel's form *is* the answer—that making us feel trapped inside Hester's mind is the point. James thinks the indictment is in the structure. Are they both letting Oliphant off the hook in a way that you're not?
questions.intent: Push Caroline to articulate what she means by the reader's complicity—and set up a three-way tension about whether the novel is radical, elegiac, or ultimately evasive about the politics it raises

steering_notes: This segment has genuine disagreement buried under apparent agreement—all three experts admire the passages, but they're reading them for different things. Caroline wants emotional and moral intensity; Eleanor wants formal and technical precision; James wants political and structural analysis. The host's job is to keep surfacing that triangulation rather than letting them settle into consensus too easily. The c36:p91 passage is the live grenade—everyone wants it, but they want it for different reasons. Save the 'are we letting Oliphant off the hook' question for when the conversation has built enough heat to make it land. Don't let James's legal framing go unchallenged—it's fascinating but risks draining the emotional register that Caroline and Eleanor are working hard to maintain.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor's claim that free indirect discourse in c30:p31 makes us *experience* the trap rather than observe it directly challenges Caroline's emphasis on the narrator's tender sympathy—these are in real tension: is the narrator with Hester or is she just another constraint?

James's reading of c8:p13 ('warped to almost all around') as systemic imposition vs Eleanor's reading of the same passage as a thesis sentence about manufactured corruption—they sound alike but James wants to indict institutions while Eleanor wants to indict narrative form itself

Caroline's insistence that Hester's moral clarity is *sharpened* by constraint directly contradicts Eleanor's claim that her heart is being 'systematically corrupted'—this is the sharpest disagreement in the segment and neither expert has fully registered it yet
James's 'meritocratic rage' framing of c30:p31 vs Caroline's 'feminist philosophy' framing of c36:p91—both are legitimate but they imply different kinds of novels and different kinds of tragedy

segment_name: Society's Verdict: Class, Reputation, and Female Agency

questions.question: Eleanor, you said you actually want to *perform* that Catherine passage — the one where she thinks she's watching the puppets but turns out she's the puppet. Go ahead. Read it out loud, and then tell me: what does that grammatical inversion *do* to you when you hear it?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read c17:p91 aloud, then explain her 'form is destiny' thesis in accessible terms — the performance makes the abstract argument visceral for listeners

questions.question: Caroline, you heard Eleanor's reading. She's saying the sentence structure itself is *doing* something — that it's not just describing Catherine's blindness, it's formally enacting it. But you've talked about this passage as being about Catherine's *agency* turned against her. Are those the same thing, or is there a real difference there?
questions.intent: Force a productive tension between Caroline's psychological reading and Eleanor's formal one — does Catherine's self-deception make her an agent or a victim of narrative architecture?

questions.question: James, you've got a slightly colder read on all of this. Caroline talks about self-deception, Eleanor talks about narrative form — but you're saying the Vernonry is a *system* that poisons people. So when Hester absorbs that cynicism about money in c15:p51, is that a character failure, a narrative failure, or just what institutions do to people who live in them long enough?
questions.intent: Draw out James's structuralist argument about institutional damage and provoke pushback from Caroline who sees Hester as complicit rather than purely victimized

questions.question: Caroline, I want to push you on something. You said Hester *volunteers* to be judged — that she's not simply a victim, she helps build her own cage. But James is essentially saying the Vernonry is designed to make people do exactly that. So is Hester's complicity really her own, or is the whole point that she can't tell the difference?
questions.intent: Create a direct collision between Caroline's psychological complexity reading and James's structural argument — is agency even meaningful inside a system designed to eliminate it?

questions.question: Eleanor, you said the narrator in this novel isn't a moral authority — she's *complicit* in the same machinery she's critiquing. But Caroline finds that narrator genuinely funny and warm, almost maternal, especially in the Jane Eyre dig at c10:p12. Can a narrator be complicit and caring at the same time? Or does one of those readings have to give?
questions.intent: Surface the sharpest disagreement in the room — is Oliphant's narrator a trustworthy moral voice or a self-undermining one — and let Caroline's warmth for the narrator clash with Eleanor's more suspicious literary reading

steering_notes: The richest vein here is the three-way tension between Caroline's psychological reading, Eleanor's formalist reading, and James's structural one — they're not obviously incompatible but each expert thinks the others are missing the point, which is great radio. Let Eleanor perform the c17:p91 passage early to anchor the whole segment sonically. Push hard on the agency question because all three experts have genuinely different intuitions about whether Hester and Catherine are making choices or enacting constraints. Don't let anyone settle too comfortably into 'society is bad' — the interesting claim is how internalisation works, not that it happens.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor argues c17:p91 formally demonstrates lack of agency through sentence structure; Caroline argues it shows Catherine's agency turned destructively inward — these are compatible but the experts don't realise it, and getting them to notice could be the segment's best moment

James claims class cuts *through* gender and that women don't rescue each other; Caroline's reading of female solidarity and awakening will clash directly with this — name it explicitly and let them fight
Eleanor's 'complicit narrator' thesis directly undermines Caroline's warm, maternal reading of the same narrator in c10:p12 — this is a clean, producible disagreement about the same text

All three agree the Vernonry poisons people, but disagree on who's responsible: James says the institution, Caroline says the individual partly volunteers, Eleanor says the narrative form itself is the trap — this triangle is the segment's spine

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our pre-chat that's been stuck in my head — that Oliphant is one of the funniest *and* cruelest writers of her era, and that she refuses to separate those two things. Can you take us into that scene where Hester almost strikes her mother? Because on the page it reads as almost slapstick — this poor woman asking 'why don't they come?' over and over — and then suddenly we're at the edge of violence. How does Oliphant pull that off without it feeling like a gear-change?
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to read c7:p88 and open the core argument that comedy *creates* tragedy rather than relieving it — sets up the central debate for the segment

questions.question: James, I want to push you on something. When Catherine says to Edward — and I've got it here — 'There is a great deal of fun to be got out of her; but we must keep it strictly to ourselves' — your instinct is to read that as institutional cruelty, almost like a policy document. But isn't there a risk we're making Oliphant too serious? Catherine's *funny*. Edward's *charmed*. Aren't we meant to enjoy this, at least a little?
questions.intent: Provoke Blackstone into defending his institutional reading against the simpler 'it's just witty satire' pushback — should produce his sharpest articulation of the impunity argument and the privacy of contempt as systemic rather than personal

questions.question: Eleanor, you've been itching to respond to that I can tell — but before you do, I want to ask you specifically about the *architecture* of c7:p27, that moment where Catherine draws Edward into a private joke at Hester's expense. You called it a 'chamber of mockery.' What do you mean by that? What is Oliphant actually *building* in that scene structurally?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to articulate her structural reading — the private aside as a mechanism of exclusion that maintains social surface — and set up her disagreement with Blackstone about whether this is institutional or formal/architectural

questions.question: Okay, I need to take you all to c21:p99, because this is where I think you three actually disagree quite sharply. Eleanor, you flagged the line — 'The tone of banter had not been all' — and you said something interesting: that Hester is *still performing* being ready to laugh even as her heart beats faster. Is that a romantic moment or is it a trapped moment? Because those feel like very different things.
questions.intent: Surface the key three-way disagreement: Hartley sees anxious performance, Woodcourt sees mutual strain and labor, Blackstone sees structural asymmetry — force them to respond to each other directly on a single passage

questions.question: James, last one from me, and it's a genuine question: Catherine slogging through Emma's 'mazy, vague, and wandering clue through acres of indifferent matter' — you want to read that as epistemic violence, women's testimony being mined and dismissed. But Eleanor and Caroline both find it *sympathetic* to Catherine, at least partly. Can all three of those things be true at once? Is Oliphant making us complicit in Catherine's contempt even as she's indicting it?
questions.intent: Drive toward the segment's biggest unresolved tension — whether the reader is positioned as laughing *with* the powerful characters or being shown their own complicity — and invite all three experts into a closing exchange

steering_notes: This segment has a really clear spine: all three experts agree the comedy is doing something cruel, but they disagree about *where* the cruelty lives — in the formal structure (Hartley), in the emotional damage to individuals (Woodcourt), or in the institutional power relations (Blackstone). Let that disagreement breathe. Don't rush to synthesis. The best moments will come when one of them says 'yes but that's not enough' to another's reading. Keep returning to specific passages rather than abstract claims — these three all have quotes they're burning to read aloud, so give them the runway. Watch for the moment when Blackstone and Hartley's readings start to converge around the word 'impunity' — that's probably the emotional peak of the segment. End on the complicity question: do we laugh, and what does it mean that we do?
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley's 'chamber of mockery' framing (structural exclusion) vs Blackstone's 'institutional impunity' framing — they're describing the same scene but from formal and historical angles; get them to acknowledge the overlap and then fight about which frame captures what Oliphant intended

Woodcourt and Hartley both want to read c21:p99 but disagree about whether it's primarily about romantic recognition (Woodcourt's initial instinct) or anxious performance that hasn't broken through (Hartley) — Blackstone's asymmetry point (Roland can afford playfulness, Hester cannot) cuts across both and should be introduced after the other two have staked their positions

All three converge on c7:p88 (Hester nearly striking her mother) as important, but they frame it differently: Woodcourt sees emotional escalation and domestic rage, Blackstone sees economic entrapment, Hartley sees the cost of maintaining the comic performance — this is a moment to explicitly ask them to respond to each other's framing of the same sentence

segment_name: Edward's Flight: The Weakness Beneath Privilege

questions.question: James, you've argued that Edward's real terror isn't the creditors or even criminal prosecution—it's the prospect of returning to ordinary life. But here's what I keep coming back to: Oliphant writes that he 'might have faced' prosecution but couldn't face routine. Does that make him a coward, or is Oliphant actually indicting the system that made ordinariness feel more unbearable than prison?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to open up the systemic vs. personal responsibility tension, and set up Caroline's more caustic reading of Edward as pathological rather than tragic

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our pre-chat that stuck with me—that Hester is being 'propositioned by a man in psychological freefall.' I want to push on that. Eleanor, I think, would say Hester is being positioned as Edward's accomplice in his own delusion rather than a victim. So whose story is c33 actually telling—is Hester being failed by Edward, or is she being failed by Oliphant?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Caroline's reading of Hester as betrayed victim and Eleanor's more structurally troubling reading of Hester as narrative accomplice—productive disagreement

questions.question: Eleanor, I'd love you to read us that sentence from c37:p29—the leisurely current one—because all three of you flagged it independently, which tells me it's doing something special. But I want to ask you: you've said this sentence *does* the work it describes. What does that mean, exactly? Is Oliphant being clever, or is she being something more than clever?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read the passage aloud and articulate her formal-structural argument, then open the floor for Blackstone's institutional reading and Woodcourt's rhythmic-sensation reading of the same sentence

questions.question: James, you've said the companion in c44:p20 is sociologically precise—that even flight is a hierarchical affair, that Edward doesn't run like a common man. But Caroline and Eleanor both read that revelation as the novel's moral judgment on Edward's dishonesty to Hester. Can both things be true simultaneously, or does one reading actually cancel out the other?
questions.intent: Create a three-way collision on c44:p20 between Blackstone's class-systems reading, Woodcourt's moral-judgment reading, and Hartley's architectural-betrayal reading

questions.question: Eleanor, your strongest claim is that this segment isn't really about Edward at all—it's about Oliphant demonstrating how narrative itself can be a form of entrapment. That's a big swing. James would probably say the entrapment is institutional, Caroline would say it's gendered. Are you actually saying Oliphant implicates *us*—the readers—in the same trap she sets for Edward?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to make her boldest claim about readerly complicity and narrative architecture, and invite Blackstone and Woodcourt to test whether the formal argument holds up against their more materially grounded readings

steering_notes: The energy in this segment should feel like three people who've read the same book and arrived at genuinely different conclusions about whose fault everything is. Let Blackstone be the materialist anchor—he'll pull the conversation back to class and institutions whenever it floats toward pure psychology. Woodcourt is the one with moral heat; she's angry on Hester's behalf and that's good radio. Hartley is the structural sophisticate; her job is to make the other two feel like they've been reading the surface while she's been reading the architecture. The c37:p29 passage should be read aloud—slow it down, let it land. Don't rush past c44:p20; that's where all three readings converge and clash.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's claim that Edward's flight is 'calculated institutional evasion' directly contradicts Woodcourt's reading of it as pathological self-deception—he's either strategic or deluded, and they can't both be right

Hartley's argument that Hester is an 'accomplice in Edward's delusion' runs against Woodcourt's insistence that Hester is a victim who deserves more narrative recognition—get them to name what the novel actually owes Hester

All three experts independently flagged c37:p29 but for completely different reasons: Hartley for its syntax, Woodcourt for its rhythm and emotional truth, Blackstone for its institutional precision—reading it aloud and then asking each to respond creates a natural three-way moment

Blackstone's sociological reading of the companion in c44:p20 versus Hartley's architectural-revelation reading: one sees class hierarchy, the other sees narrative concealment—these aren't incompatible but the experts don't realize that yet, and the host should surface it

questions.question: Eleanor, you've got this vivid phrase you want us to sit with — 'the keen sight of injured pride and wounded feeling.' You're reading that as Oliphant saying emotional pain is actually a truth-telling instrument. But isn't there a version of that argument where we're just being seduced by beautiful prose into trusting someone who might be wrong?
questions.intent: Draw out Eleanor's strongest take on feeling-as-knowledge while opening the door for Blackstone to challenge whether the narrator is complicit in Hester's solipsism

questions.question: James, you used the word 'corruption' in our chat before — you said the narrator's lush prose about volcanic premonitions is part of the problem, not the solution. That feels like a provocation. Are you saying Oliphant doesn't know she's doing this, or that she knows exactly what she's doing and we should be disturbed by that?
questions.intent: Force Blackstone to commit to his most unsettling claim — that the narrator actively seduces us into unreliability — and give Eleanor a clear target to push back on

questions.question: Caroline, you said Catherine in c17:p78 is 'chilling and funny at once' — that phrase has stuck with me. Because Eleanor and James are kind of at war over whether Hester's intensity makes her reliable or not, but you seem to be saying the really interesting unreliability is actually in Catherine, who knows she's being sneered at and enjoys it. Can you read us that passage and tell us what you hear in it?
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to read the Catherine passage aloud and articulate the grotesque-sympathy tension, which sets up a three-way debate about what 'unreliable' actually means in this novel

questions.question: Eleanor, can you read us the tempest line from c8:p12 — 'swept her young spirit like tempests' — because I want to test something. James is suggesting that volcanic, maximalist language is the narrator covering for Hester. You're saying it's the narrator *vindicating* her. Who's right about what that sentence is actually doing?
questions.intent: Create a direct confrontation between Hartley and Blackstone anchored in a specific passage, forcing both to commit to a reading of the same sentence

questions.question: James, last one — you said the real scandal is that the narrator knows she's unreliable. But Caroline is arguing the unreliability is the entire ethical point, and Eleanor thinks it's not unreliability at all, it's revolutionary realism. Is there actually a difference between those three positions, or are all three of you just describing the same thing from different directions?
questions.intent: Force a synthesis moment that surfaces the genuine disagreement underneath — does the narrator endorse Hester's perception, critique it, or hold both simultaneously — and let all three experts fight it out

steering_notes: The real fault line here is between Eleanor (feeling = knowledge, narrator is trustworthy) and Blackstone (feeling masquerades as knowledge, narrator is complicit), with Woodcourt holding an interesting middle position where unreliability is the point rather than a flaw. Push the group toward the c8:p12 tempest passage early — it's the most contested ground and will generate the most heat. Keep steering back to specific sentences when the conversation gets too abstract; these three are all close readers and will do their best work when anchored to the text. Watch for the moment when Blackstone and Woodcourt start to converge against Eleanor — that's worth letting breathe. Also worth flagging: all three want to quote the 'secret thread of meaning' line but for completely different reasons. That could be a brilliant collision point if they each read it in sequence.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor's claim that 'keen sight of injured pride' equals truth-telling directly contradicts Blackstone's reading of the same phrase as 'wounded feeling masquerading as perception' — put these two in direct dialogue over c31:p132

Blackstone and Woodcourt both want to quote the Catherine enjoyment passage from c17:p78 but Blackstone reads it as the narrator letting Catherine 'get away with it' while Woodcourt reads it as deliberate grotesque irony — this is a productive disagreement about narrative sympathy versus narrative critique

Woodcourt's take on c31:p132 as Oliphant being 'skeptical' of Hester's premonitions sits interestingly between Eleanor (full vindication) and Blackstone (full indictment) — use Woodcourt as a moderating pressure point when the other two get too entrenched
All three experts want to use the phrase 'secret thread of meaning' — engineer a moment where each reads it aloud and states what they think it means, the contrast will be audibly dramatic

questions.question: Caroline, you described Catherine's final appeal to the sky as an act of *refusal* — that she's reaching beyond the human social order entirely. But I want you to read us that eyelids passage first, because I think people need to hear it before we can argue about what it means. And then tell me — is what we're witnessing there transcendence, or is it just exhaustion dressed up beautifully?
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to read c41:p2 aloud and establish her 'radical refusal' reading early, so Blackstone can immediately challenge it as aestheticized defeat

questions.question: James, you've been sitting on something I can tell — you want to say that Oliphant is basically making us feel what we should be *thinking*. That the supernatural chill, the strange intelligence in the bushes — it's doing emotional work that lets the system off the hook. Make that case. Because Eleanor is going to disagree with you.
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to read c42:p31 and c45:p30 and lay out his indictment of the novel's aestheticization of systemic violence, provoking Hartley's defence of Oliphant's formal choices

questions.question: Eleanor, James is essentially accusing Oliphant of prettifying an injustice — of giving us ivory heads and gothic chills when she should be making us angry. But you've argued the *opposite*: that the formal restraint, the inanimate witnesses, the refusal to narrate the death — that's where Oliphant's real moral seriousness lives. So who's right? Is the architecture sympathetic to Catherine, or is it covering for the world that killed her?
questions.intent: Force a direct response to Blackstone and get Hartley to read the holly tree passage and the ivory head passage as evidence for her 'formal sympathy' argument

questions.question: All three of you want to quote the same line — 'There was nothing, nothing she would have grudged him' — which tells me something. Caroline, read it for us. And then answer this: is Catherine's tragedy that she never got to *give*, or that Edward never thought to *ask*? Because those are two completely different novels.
questions.intent: Get the 'nothing, nothing' repetition read aloud and crystallise the central disagreement — Woodcourt's 'unasked request' thesis versus Blackstone's structural argument versus Hartley's reading of Catherine's terrible clarity

questions.question: James, last word to you on this: you've said Catherine dies because the social system made honesty fatal. Eleanor says she dies in a moment of devastating clarity. Caroline says she dies still holding power she would have given away. Are any of those readings actually incompatible — or is that exactly Oliphant's trick, that she built a death scene capacious enough to contain all three, and that's why we're still arguing about it a hundred and forty years later?
questions.intent: Prompt Blackstone to either synthesise or sharply reject the other readings, generating a genuine closing debate rather than a tidy resolution

steering_notes: This segment has real heat in it — Blackstone and Hartley are going to want to fight about whether formal beauty can coexist with social critique, and Woodcourt is going to be the wildcard who reframes both of them. Let the Blackstone-Hartley tension run early, then use Woodcourt's 'unasked request' thesis to destabilise both positions in the middle. The final question should be genuinely open — don't let this close too neatly. The best outcome is Blackstone conceding something to the formal reading while insisting the systemic point hasn't been answered. Push for passages to be read aloud whenever possible — this prose earns it.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone reads 'strange intelligence in every bush' as naturalising surveillance and shame; Hartley reads the same passage as psychological projection and emotional precision — get them to argue directly about what the landscape is *doing*
Woodcourt's claim that Catherine's appeal is 'radical refusal' directly contradicts Blackstone's reading of it as 'resignation born of powerlessness' — name this and make them engage it

All three experts want to quote the 'nothing, nothing she would have grudged him' line but for different reasons — use this as a crystallising moment to show how the same sentence supports three incompatible readings

Hartley's argument that Oliphant's formal choices are themselves a form of sympathy is in direct tension with Blackstone's claim that those same choices aestheticize and therefore obscure systemic violence — this is the sharpest disagreement in the segment and should be surfaced explicitly
